subtopic_detail: Separating suture fusion from positional moulding by ear position and contralateral bossing
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5 month old boy whose parents have noticed that the back of his head has looked uneven since about two months of age and has not improved despite them alternating the side he is laid down on.

He was born at term by normal vaginal birth and has met his milestones. His head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile since birth. On examination the right side of the back of his head is flattened. His right ear sits further back and slightly lower than the left. The forehead on the left side is more prominent than the right, and there is a firm ridge you can feel running from the back of the skull towards the right ear with a bony fullness behind that ear. He turns his head freely to both sides with no tightness in the neck.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening, right ear displaced posteriorly and inferiorly, contralateral left frontal bossing, palpable ridge over the right lambdoid suture with an ipsilateral mastoid bulge, full passive neck rotation both ways, head circumference on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Development age appropriate, red reflexes present bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for a moulding helmet and review again in three months
options.rationale: Helmet therapy remodels a skull whose sutures are open and cannot correct a fused suture, so it would waste the months in which surgical correction gives the best cosmetic and functional result (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons).
source_refs: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for neck stretches and review in a month
options.rationale: Congenital muscular torticollis commonly underlies positional flattening and responds to stretching, but his neck rotates fully in both directions so there is no restriction to treat (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Arrange skull radiographs and review the films in the clinic
options.rationale: Plain films are insensitive for partial fusion and normal images would falsely reassure, so imaging decisions belong to the craniofacial team who use low dose computed tomography with three dimensional reconstruction (Source: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons).
source_refs: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons

options.text: Refer to a craniofacial service for urgent specialist assessment
options.rationale: A palpable sutural ridge with the ear displaced posteriorly, bossing on the opposite forehead and a mastoid bulge gives the trapezoid head shape of a fused suture rather than the parallelogram of positional moulding, and this requires craniofacial assessment because surgical correction is time critical (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Advise repositioning and tummy time with review in three months
options.rationale: Repositioning is the correct treatment for the near pair, positional plagiocephaly, but that condition pushes the ear forwards on the flattened side and produces bossing of the forehead on the same side rather than the opposite one (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Abnormal head shape in infancy is overwhelmingly positional and has become much more common since supine sleeping was recommended, but a small proportion reflects premature fusion of a cranial suture and that group needs surgery. The two are separated at the bedside rather than radiologically: positional flattening produces a parallelogram with the ear and forehead pushed forward on the flattened side, while lambdoid fusion produces a trapezoid with the ear pulled back and down and bossing of the opposite forehead. A palpable ridge over the suture and a bulge behind the ear are additional pointers to fusion. Sagittal fusion is the commonest single suture form and produces a long narrow head, while fusion of multiple sutures raises intracranial pressure and threatens vision and development.
key_points: Positional flattening gives a parallelogram with the ipsilateral ear and forehead pushed forwards.
Lambdoid fusion gives a trapezoid with the ipsilateral ear pulled backwards and downwards.
Contralateral frontal bossing and a mastoid bulge point to fusion rather than moulding.
A palpable ridge along a suture line is an important physical sign.
Referral is time critical because early surgery gives the best result.
explanation.pearls: Head circumference crossing centiles downwards, a bulging fontanelle or new developmental regression suggest multiple suture involvement with raised intracranial pressure, and that combination warrants same day rather than routine specialist referral.

subtopic_detail: Observation rather than treatment for isolated thrombocytopenia with cutaneous bleeding only
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4 year old boy brought in by his father because of bruises. Over three days he has developed dozens of bruises on both shins and forearms and a rash of tiny red spots across his chest and back that do not fade when pressed.

He had a runny nose and cough a fortnight ago that settled without treatment. He had one nosebleed yesterday that stopped after five minutes of pressure. He has been running around the waiting room and eating a sandwich while you take the history. There is no fever today, no bone or joint pain, no night waking and no weight loss. There is no lymphadenopathy and no palpable liver or spleen edge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae over trunk and limbs, bruises over both shins and forearms, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bone tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 12 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 121 g/L (110-140), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), neutrophils 3.1 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), blood film shows large platelets with normal red and white cell morphology and no blasts

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin followed by early outpatient review
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin raises the count within 24 to 48 hours and is reserved for significant mucosal bleeding or an urgent need to raise the count, neither of which applies to a single self limiting nosebleed (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Oral prednisolone for four days with early outpatient review
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is an alternative first line agent when treatment is indicated, but giving it before the marrow has been considered risks partially treating an undiagnosed leukaemia and altering its appearance (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Platelet transfusion followed by admission for overnight observation
options.rationale: Transfused platelets are destroyed by the same autoantibody within hours, so transfusion is reserved for life threatening haemorrhage alongside immunoglobulin and corticosteroid (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate before any treatment decision is made
options.rationale: Marrow examination is the near pair and is indicated when there are atypical features such as anaemia, neutropenia, blasts on the film, organomegaly or bone pain, and this child has an otherwise entirely normal count and film (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Observation with written safety advice and early outpatient review
options.rationale: Treatment is directed at bleeding rather than at the platelet count, and a well child with skin and mild mucosal bleeding only is managed expectantly with written advice about avoiding contact sport and non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs, since around 80 per cent recover spontaneously within six months (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Immune thrombocytopenia in children is typically a post viral, self limiting illness with an abrupt onset in a child who is otherwise entirely well, which is precisely what distinguishes it from marrow failure or infiltration. The count often sits below 20 x10^9/L, but serious bleeding is uncommon and intracranial haemorrhage occurs in well under one per cent, so the decision to treat is driven by the bleeding phenotype rather than the number. Features that should prompt marrow examination include any other cytopenia, abnormal cells on the film, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bone pain or systemic symptoms. Families need written information because the reassurance that a very low count is compatible with home management is counterintuitive and often gets lost.
key_points: Treatment is based on bleeding severity, not on the platelet count alone.
A well child with skin and mild mucosal bleeding is managed with observation.
Anaemia, neutropenia, blasts, organomegaly or bone pain point away from the diagnosis and towards marrow examination.
Around 80 per cent of children recover spontaneously within six months.
Advice covers avoidance of contact sport, non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and aspirin.
explanation.pearls: Non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and aspirin are avoided for the duration of the thrombocytopenia because they add a functional platelet defect to a quantitative one, and paracetamol is the analgesic of choice in these children.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines
Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Acting on an intermediate predictor score in an irritable hip rather than waiting for every criterion
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 3 year old boy who has refused to stand since yesterday morning. His mother says he screams if anyone moves his right leg and that he had a runny nose last week that has settled.

He lies with the right hip flexed and turned outwards and cries with any attempt to move it. He is drinking and interactive between examinations. There is no rash, no other joint involvement and no history of trauma. A hip ultrasound performed in the department shows a moderate right hip effusion with no effusion on the left.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear, right hip held flexed and externally rotated, marked pain on passive internal rotation, no rash and no other joint involvement
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.5 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/hr (less than 15), blood culture collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent ultrasound guided hip aspiration before antibiotics are given
options.rationale: Three of the four clinical predictors are met with a C reactive protein of 42 mg/L, which alone carries a high likelihood of infection, and joint fluid must be obtained before antibiotics because culture yield falls sharply once treatment starts (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin now and arrange aspiration tomorrow
options.rationale: Treating first is understandable but sterilises the joint fluid and leaves the organism and its sensitivities unknown for a course that will run for several weeks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Admit for observation with analgesia and repeat bloods in 12 hours
options.rationale: Observation is the pathway for transient synovitis, but that child is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers and will weight bear, and delay here risks femoral head destruction within a day (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and general practice review in 48 hours
options.rationale: A temperature just below one predictor threshold does not make the overall picture benign, and discharging a febrile child who will not weight bear with a raised C reactive protein is the classic error in this presentation (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis before aspiration
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is the near pair and is valuable for detecting adjacent osteomyelitis or a pelvic collection, but it requires sedation and should not delay aspiration when the joint effusion is already demonstrated (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: The irritable hip in a young child sits on a spectrum from transient synovitis, which needs analgesia and review, to septic arthritis, which needs washout within hours. The four predictors of fever, refusal to weight bear, erythrocyte sedimentation rate above 40 mm/hr and white cell count above 12 x10^9/L were derived to help, but they were never intended to be applied as a pass or fail rule, and a child meeting three of four has a probability of infection well above 90 per cent in the original series. C reactive protein was not in the original set and has since emerged as the single strongest laboratory predictor, with values above 20 mg/L substantially raising the odds. Aspiration before antibiotics preserves the culture, and delayed treatment in a septic hip leads to avascular necrosis and permanent joint destruction because the femoral head blood supply runs inside the capsule.
key_points: Refusal to weight bear plus fever plus raised inflammatory markers indicates aspiration, not observation.
The four predictor score is a probability aid rather than a threshold rule.
C reactive protein above 20 mg/L is the strongest single laboratory predictor.
Joint fluid is obtained before antibiotics wherever possible to preserve culture yield.
The intracapsular femoral head blood supply makes delay in the hip particularly damaging.
explanation.pearls: In a child under three months, or one who is immunised incompletely or immunosuppressed, empirical cover is broadened beyond staphylococcal cover because Kingella kingae and Haemophilus influenzae type b become realistic pathogens and both are easily missed on routine culture.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Deciding oral against intravenous therapy for eyelid cellulitis on the basis of eye examination findings
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 5 year old girl with two days of a red swollen right upper eyelid that started after her mother noticed an insect bite there.

The swelling has increased so that she now holds the eye half closed, though she opens it fully when asked. Her mother has held her home from school but reports she has eaten normally and been her usual self. Holding the lids apart, the conjunctiva is white, the eye moves fully in all directions without pain, the pupil reacts briskly with no relative afferent defect, and she reads the same line on the chart with each eye. The globe does not protrude and the redness stops at the bony rim of the orbit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right upper lid swelling and erythema confined within the orbital rim, no proptosis, full painless extraocular movements, no relative afferent pupillary defect, equal visual acuity both eyes, no chemosis
data_table.Investigations: Immunisations up to date including Haemophilus influenzae type b

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol drops with review again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Topical treatment reaches the conjunctival surface rather than the eyelid soft tissue, and the conjunctiva here is white, so the target of the drops is not the site of infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Referral to ophthalmology for examination within the next week
options.rationale: A week is far too long an interval for a condition that can cross the septum within a day, and the eye examination that ophthalmology would perform has already been completed and is normal (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Oral antibiotics as an outpatient with review again in 24 hours
options.rationale: Infection confined anterior to the orbital septum in a systemically well child over one year, with a fully assessable and normal eye, is treated with oral antibiotics and mandatory review the next day to detect progression (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Admission for intravenous antibiotics and review again in 24 hours
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy is indicated where the eye cannot be assessed, the child is under one year or systemically unwell, or any orbital sign is present, and none of those applies here (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Computed tomography of the orbits before any antibiotic is started
options.rationale: Imaging is the near pair reserved for suspected postseptal disease or a subperiosteal collection, signalled by proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, chemosis or reduced acuity, and it delivers a radiation dose to the developing lens for no benefit here (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: The orbital septum is the anatomical divide that determines management of periocular infection. Anterior to it, infection is confined to the lid and behaves like any soft tissue cellulitis; posterior to it, infection sits in the orbit, threatens the optic nerve and can spread to the cavernous sinus. The distinction is clinical, resting on proptosis, pain or restriction of eye movement, chemosis, reduced acuity and a relative afferent pupillary defect, and it is unreliable if the child will not allow the lids to be parted. Preseptal disease most often follows local trauma, an insect bite or a lid lesion, whereas postseptal disease usually arises from ethmoid sinusitis, which is why the two present at different ages and with different histories.
key_points: Painless full eye movements, normal acuity and absent proptosis place the infection anterior to the septum.
Oral therapy with 24 hour review is appropriate for a well child over one year with a normal eye examination.
Intravenous therapy is required if the eye cannot be assessed or any orbital sign is present.
Imaging is reserved for suspected postseptal infection or a subperiosteal collection.
Preseptal disease follows local skin breach; postseptal disease usually follows ethmoid sinusitis.
explanation.pearls: If a distressed child will not let you open the lids, that alone converts the case to the intravenous pathway, because an unassessable eye must be treated as though it harbours postseptal disease until proven otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Using a raised gonadotrophin to redirect the investigation of short stature with absent puberty
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 14 year old girl referred because she is the shortest in her year and has not started her periods.

She is doing well academically and has no headaches, no visual symptoms and no change in appetite or bowel habit. Her height is 143 cm, below the 1st centile, and the growth chart shows her height velocity falling away from her centile line from about eight years of age. Her mother is 168 cm and her father is 178 cm. There is no breast tissue, but she has sparse pubic and axillary hair. Her chest is broad with widely spaced nipples, the hairline at the back of her neck sits low, and her elbows carry outwards when her arms are held straight. Blood pressure is equal in both arms and femoral pulses are easily felt.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg in both arms, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Height 143 cm below the 1st centile, weight on the 25th centile, Tanner stage 1 breast development with Tanner stage 3 pubic hair, low posterior hairline, broad chest, cubitus valgus, multiple pigmented naevi
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 68 IU/L (1-9 in the prepubertal range), luteinising hormone 24 IU/L (0.1-6), oestradiol less than 40 pmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), insulin like growth factor 1 within the normal range for age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Send coeliac serology and thyroid function as the next tests
options.rationale: Coeliac disease and hypothyroidism are the standard screens for short stature with delayed puberty and are the near pair here, but the thyroid function is already normal and neither raises the follicle stimulating hormone (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines).
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Send a peripheral blood karyotype as the next investigation
options.rationale: A markedly raised follicle stimulating hormone places the defect in the ovary rather than the pituitary, and primary ovarian failure with short stature and these physical features in a phenotypic girl is investigated by karyotype, which also identifies mosaicism and any Y chromosome material (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary region
options.rationale: Imaging the pituitary is the right move when gonadotrophins are low or inappropriately normal alongside a low oestradiol, and hers are high, which excludes a central cause (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group

options.text: Arrange a growth hormone stimulation test before other tests
options.rationale: Growth hormone deficiency is the tempting explanation for a falling height velocity, but the insulin like growth factor 1 is normal and it would not explain the raised gonadotrophins or the physical features (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group

options.text: Start transdermal oestradiol replacement and review in a year
options.rationale: Oestrogen replacement will be needed, but starting it before the karyotype forfeits the chance to plan growth promoting treatment and to screen for the cardiac, renal and autoimmune associations that the diagnosis carries (Source: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).
source_refs: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group

explanation.summary: Short stature with absent puberty is separated first by the gonadotrophins: high values indicate primary gonadal failure, while low or normal values indicate a hypothalamic or pituitary cause or constitutional delay. Turner syndrome affects around one in 2500 live born girls and is frequently diagnosed late, because the physical features can be subtle and adrenarche proceeds normally, so pubic and axillary hair develop and give a false impression that puberty has begun. Growth failure typically becomes evident in mid childhood, well before the absent breast development declares itself, and growth hormone therapy started early adds several centimetres to adult height. Diagnosis triggers a defined surveillance programme covering the bicuspid aortic valve and aortic coarctation, renal tract anomalies, hearing, thyroid autoimmunity, coeliac disease and later fertility planning.
key_points: A raised follicle stimulating hormone localises the problem to the gonad and excludes a central cause.
Adrenarche is normal in Turner syndrome, so pubic and axillary hair can mislead.
Karyotype identifies mosaicism and Y chromosome material, which carries gonadoblastoma risk.
Cardiac, renal, thyroid, coeliac and hearing surveillance all begin at diagnosis.
Growth hormone therapy started early increases final adult height.
explanation.pearls: Around 5 to 10 per cent of girls with Turner syndrome have aortic coarctation and up to 30 per cent a bicuspid aortic valve, so echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging are arranged at diagnosis even when femoral pulses and four limb blood pressures are normal.
